3.3. Discussion
Experiment 2, like Experiment 1, examined how emphasizing com-
mon ingroup, or dual identities instead of different group identity in it-
self affects motivation for collective action. The results of Experiment 2
replicated the key results from Experiment 1: (a) compared to a focus
on separate identities, common ingroup identity group reduced anger,
group-efﬁcacy beliefs, and, consequently (based on our path models),
collective action intentions among disadvantaged-group members
(ds = .43–.58); (b) compared to separate group identity, dual identity
did not reduce (but also not increase) anger, group-efﬁcacy beliefs,
and collective action intentions (ds = .04–.18); and (c) compared to
dual identity, common ingroup identity reduced motivation for collec-
tive action (Cohen's d = .48) and group-efﬁcacy beliefs (d = .43); the
effect for group anger was similar but weaker (d = .36). The results of
both experiments converge and contribute to the extant literature by
showing that some interventions to promote intergroup harmony

mately half of the sample and had relatively good sleep quality,
few sleep disturbances, and a low percentage of short and long

quality classes (which accounted for 39.2% of the sample) indi-

sleep durations and frequent sleep disturbances. The implications
of Long Sleepers (9.6%) are less clear, as this class could include
a mix of good and poor sleepers. Some individuals, for instance,
may have a greater physiological sleep need which results in

interaction with coherence of narration was significant (with both
Fs  1). Thus, although the participants were able to compensate
for coherence breaks in the narration by attending to the accom-
panying moving pictures on a local level, their overall compre-
hension of the film was nevertheless disturbed.
